newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cuba accuses U.S. of "biological aggression".
newsitem.headline: Cuba accuses U.S. of "biological aggression".

text.p: Cuba has accused the United States of "biological aggression," saying a plague of plant-destroying insects first appeared in the west of the country after a U.S. crop-dusting plane was seen spraying unknown substances during a flight over the region.

In a note to Secretary-General Kofi Annan published on Monday, Cuba identified the pest as Thrips palmi, which it said "strikes and severely damages practically every crop, and is also resistant to a considerable variety of pesticides."
For this reason the insects, which had spread widely in western Cuba, "can be considered ideal biological agents able to inflict heavy damage on agricultural food crops."
Cuba said the first signs of a "Thrips plague" appeared in potato plantations on the Lenin state horticultural farm in Matanzas province on Dec. 18 last year.

It said this followed the sighting over Matanzas province on Oct. 21 of a single-engine civilian S2R crop-dusting plane operated by the U.S. State Department which, according to the pilot of a Cuban Airlines Fokker aircraft, released "unknown substances, in the form of a white or grayish mist."

"Bearing in mind the reproductive cycle of this insect, the beginning of the infection can be ascertained as approximately Oct. 21, 1996, which was precisely the date when the United States S2R aircraft flew over this point."
Cuba said the U.S. plane, used in "the struggle against drug trafficking, to destroy crops," took off from Patrick Air Force base in Cocoa Beach, Florida, bound for Grand Cayman island.

"The analysis of the facts and the results of the investigations allow us to relate, with a high degree of accuracy, the appearance of Thrips palmi in Matanzas province with the dropping on Oct. 21, 1996, of an unknown substance by an aircraft operated by the United States State Department," the Cuban note said.
"There is reliable evidence that Cuba has once again been the target of biological aggression," it added.
An official at the U.S. mission to the United Nations, asked for comment on the Cuban allegation, said: "The United States is not engaged in any biological warfare or insect infestation in Cuba."

The Cuban note said that while the pest had appeared since 1985 in Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica, the fact it did not occur in neighbouring eastern Cuba but in western Cuba, more than 375 miles (600 km) away, was "odd and suspicious."

Cuba said it complained to the U.S. interests section in Havana on Dec. 26 and asked for clarification. It was told on Feb. 12, 1997, that the U.S. pilot had spotted a Cuban commercial airliner flying below. As he was not certain of having been seen, the pilot "used the 'smoke generator' of his aircraft, in order to indicate its location."
The U.S. reply added that "the smoke vanished and no fluid was poured from the airplane."

Cuba said no smoke generator was known to be installed on that aircraft and that the U.S. explanation "appears, from the technical point of view, weak and in contradiction with the conversation held during the flight."
The Cuban pilot was also quoted as saying the U.S. plane did not release smoke but "a substance."

"At present, Thrips palmi is spread virtually throughout Matanzas and La Habana provinces, in two municipalities of Cienfuegos province, in some municipalities of Pinar Del Rio province and in the Island of Youth. Its presence has not been detected in the central and eastern provinces of the country," the note said.
